name: Bilal Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Bilal. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything here is confidential, so you can tell me your public line and, separately, what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the office administrator at Halden and Price, a small architecture practice with fourteen people above a bakery on Mill Lane. I handle the diary, client meetings, invoices, the planning application paperwork and keeping the printer alive. About half of that I've already handed to AI tools I set up myself, so most mornings I'm checking what they did overnight rather than doing it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like building the little systems, like the one that chases unpaid invoices politely after 30 days, then less politely after 45. What wears me out is the architects, bless them, who still send me photos of handwritten notes and expect them typed. I use AI tools every single day, for everything from minutes to sorting planning documents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was useful but overhyped, which is what I've basically said all along. I'd post something like that on my professional profile. I'd also say the time saved should go to staff, as shorter weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fine. My tools would keep saving me a couple of hours a day, and the practice would still need someone who knows how all of it works. I'd probably be a bit bored, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep refining my automations and maybe pitch a four-day week to the partners, since I've freed up time. I'd keep putting money into my index fund every month like I do now. I might sell a few of my set-ups to friends' small offices on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little flat. I was ready for a revolution and got a slightly better spreadsheet, which is honestly fine for my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The four-day week pitch. How would the partners react?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Halden would say no on the spot, and Ms Price would say let's trial it. I'd bring the numbers: hours saved per week since I brought the tools in. It's about who gets the time AI frees up, and I think it should be the staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything about this picture on your mind at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that I'd stall a bit. I'm 27 and I've made my name at work as the AI person. If AI stays small, I'm just an administrator who's good with software, which is fine but not where I wanted to be.

say: I'd say AI was **useful but overhyped**, as I've said all along.
I'd argue the saved time should go to staff as **shorter weeks**.
think: My tools would keep saving **two hours a day**, and the practice still needs me to run them.
If anything I'd feel a bit **stalled** in my career.
do: Keep refining his **automations** at the practice.
Pitch a **four-day week** to the partners with hours-saved numbers.
Sell set-ups to **friends' small offices** on the side.
feel: **Calm**, slightly flat, a bit let down that nothing bigger came.
S0.quote: I was ready for a revolution and got a slightly better spreadsheet, which is honestly fine for my rent.
fieldNote: Bilal is already **halfway automated** and runs the tools himself.
His progressive view shows in asking who gets the **freed time**.
His only worry is **career stall**, not job loss.

steps.text: Keep refining the invoice and diary automations at the practice
Set up invoice-chasing tools for friends' small offices for a fee
Keep paying into the index fund each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make sure the gains are shared, not just kept by owners. At work I'd say I'm happy to lead the change but I want staff to have a say. Online I'd write about how I've done it at a small firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is my best picture. I'm already doing what the card describes, so I'd be the one other offices hire. The admin role as it is now shrinks, but I'd move into running the systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners to make me operations manager, with a pay rise, since I'd be replacing the work of a second hire. I'd take an online course in workflow automation in the first six months. And I'd start charging for small office set-ups properly, maybe two clients a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit guilty, because I know other administrators wouldn't be so lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned guilt. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Marisol does admin at a dental surgery and hates computers. The same change that gets me a promotion could cost my cousin Marisol her job, and that doesn't sit right with me. I'd probably end up teaching Marisol on Sunday afternoons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry the systems you build could replace you too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. But someone still has to choose the tools, check them and fix them when they break. In this picture there's time to keep moving up.

say: I'd say the gains must be **shared with staff**, not kept by owners.
I'd offer to **lead the change** at work as long as staff get a say.
think: This is my **best picture**, since I already do what the card describes.
The admin role shrinks, but I'd move into **running the systems**.
do: Ask the partners for an **operations manager** title and a pay rise.
Take an online **workflow automation** course in the first six months.
Charge for **office set-ups** properly, about two clients a month.
feel: **Excited**, with some guilt about administrators who won't be as lucky.
S1.quote: The same change that gets me a promotion could cost my cousin Marisol her job, and that doesn't sit right with me.
fieldNote: Bilal sees Steady Disruption as a **promotion route**, not a threat.
His **guilt** about his cousin shows his progressive values are personal.
He admits his own **systems** could replace him eventually.

steps.text: Ask the partners for an operations manager role and pay rise
Complete an online workflow automation course within six months
Charge two small offices a month for AI admin set-ups
Teach cousin Marisol the booking tools on Sundays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this has to come with a basic income, straight away, because nobody can adjust in two years. I'd post about it and I'd sign every petition. I'd say the companies that built it should pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my edge disappears. If the AI can do any thinking job, it can also set up the tools and fix them, which is my whole advantage. I'd have maybe a year of being useful as the person who plugs it in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell my set-up service hard for that first year, because every small office would want help in the panic. I'd put most of what I earned into savings and keep the index fund going. In parallel I'd look at something hands-on, maybe a trade course, for the three years before robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, which is new for me. For the first time the thing I'm always early on is coming for the thing I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd look at a trade. Which one, and how seriously?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Electrician, probably, because my uncle Tiago does it and says there's never enough of them. But it's a four-year apprenticeship and the robots come in three. So I'd be serious, but I'd know it's a bridge, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You have a good cushion. How much does that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot, honestly. I have about a year of rent and food saved plus the index fund. I could take a pay cut to train without panicking, which most people couldn't.

say: I'd demand a **basic income** at once, because nobody can adjust in two years.
I'd say the **companies that built it** should pay for it.
think: My **edge disappears** once AI can set up and fix its own tools.
I'd get maybe **one year** of being useful as the person who plugs it in.
do: Sell his **set-up service** hard during the first year's rush.
Save most of those **extra earnings** and keep the index fund going.
Look at an **electrician course** as a bridge before robots arrive.
feel: **Nervous**, which is new for him, as AI reaches his own strength.
S2.quote: For the first time the thing I'm always early on is coming for the thing I'm good at.
fieldNote: Bilal sees his **advantage vanish** because AGI can do the setting up too.
He treats a trade as a **bridge**, knowing robots follow in three years.
His **strong cushion** gives him room to take a pay cut and train.

steps.text: Sell AI set-ups to small offices during the first-year rush
Bank most of the extra earnings in savings
Apply for an electrician course with uncle Tiago's help
Sign and share basic income petitions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is the time to build a proper public plan, and I'd want my profession body and unions to push for it. I'd post practical guides for other office staff. I'd stay positive in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is a decent run for me. I'd ride the change for three or four years as the systems person, then the AI does that too. So the question is what I build with the money from those years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the operations manager job and get the pay rise in year one. I'd grow the side business to steady income and save half of it. I'd also start thinking seriously about co-owning something, maybe a small co-op office service with two friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fired up and a bit worried at the same time. It's like a race with a clear finish line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A co-op office service. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three of us, each owning a third, running AI admin for small firms on Mill Lane and around. We'd split profits evenly. If machines are going to do the office work, I'd rather the people who used to do it own the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to that co-op when AGI arrives in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it probably gets squeezed too. But owning something is better than being paid by the hour for something that disappears. And by then we'd have savings to fall back on.

say: I'd say five years is time to build a **public plan**, pushed by unions.
I'd post **practical guides** for other office staff and stay positive.
think: I'd ride the change for **three or four years** as the systems person.
The real question is what I **build with the money** from those years.
do: Take the **operations manager** job and pay rise in year one.
Grow the **side business** and save half of it.
Plan a small **office services co-op** with two friends.
feel: **Fired up and worried**, like a race with a clear finish line.
S3.quote: If machines are going to do the office work, I'd rather the people who used to do it own the machines.
fieldNote: Bilal turns five years into a plan to **earn, save and own**.
His **co-op idea** puts his progressive politics into practice.
He still expects his **systems role** to end around 2031.

steps.text: Take the operations manager role and its pay rise
Save half of the side business income each month
Set up an office services co-op with two friends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for a fair transition if governments start now, with retraining and a basic income trial. I'd write about it and go to local meetings. I'd be hopeful in public, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is great for me. I'd have a decade of being in demand, and I'd be 37 at the end, with money saved. That's a lot of runway to work out what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do everything from the five-year picture but slower: the operations job, the side work, the co-op. I'd also look at a part-time degree in something human-facing, like urban planning, which links to the architecture work. And I'd keep investing every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a little restless. Ten years is long enough to build something, so I'd spend those years building instead of worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Urban planning is still thinking work. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. I like it because it's about people arguing over their streets, and that part's political, not technical. I think people will want humans in those rooms for a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The administrators who are my age but don't like tech, like Marisol. Ten years is plenty, but only if someone actually helps them. That's where I'd want the government money to go.

say: I'd say a decade allows a **fair transition** if governments start now.
I'd back a **basic income trial** and go to local meetings.
think: Ten years means a **decade of demand** for my skills.
At **37** with savings, I'd have plenty of runway.
do: Pursue the **operations job**, side work and co-op at a slower pace.
Start a part-time degree in **urban planning**.
feel: **Calm** and a little **restless**, eager to build rather than worry.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to build something, so I'd spend those years building instead of worrying.
fieldNote: Bilal sees ten years as a **runway**, not a threat.
He picks **urban planning** for its human, political side, not its tasks.
He worries most about **tech-shy peers** like his cousin.

steps.text: Start a part-time urban planning degree in year one
Keep paying into the index fund every month
Go to local council meetings about a basic income trial

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Even with my savings and skills, two years means the thing I'm good at stops mattering almost at once. What would help is a basic income starting the day it arrives, paid for by the AI companies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the tools. Being good at AI only protects you until AI is good at AI, so owning a share of the work matters more than skill.

headlineQuote: Being good at AI only protects you until AI is good at AI, so owning a share of the work matters more than skill.
portrait: Bilal is a 27-year-old **architecture practice administrator** who has automated half his own job.
He uses AI **every day** and builds tools for friends' offices on the side.
He sees Steady Disruption as a **promotion**, but AGI erodes his edge.
His **progressive** views push him towards basic income and a co-op he'd co-own.
A **strong cushion** lets him retrain without panic.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his core skill stops mattering almost at once.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** from day one, paid for by the AI companies.
